summary: SCTP carries multiple streams in one connection but large messages can block others. This document adds a new chunk type that lets a sender interleave pieces of different user messages, and defines stream schedulers that decide which stream sends next.

eli5.summary: If one person hogs the line at the checkout, everyone waits. This lets the cashier serve a bit of each person's order in turn.

questions: how to interleave messages in sctp
what is the sctp i-data chunk
how does sctp message interleaving work
what stream schedulers does sctp have
why does webrtc need sctp interleaving
subtitle: A new SCTP chunk lets a sender mix pieces of different messages, plus a menu of schedulers for choosing which stream goes next.

tldr.problem: In SCTP a large message must go out in consecutive chunks, so one big message on one stream can block every other stream at the sender.
tldr.mechanism: A new I-DATA chunk carries a Message Identifier and a Fragment Sequence Number so fragments no longer depend on consecutive TSNs, and several stream schedulers decide which stream sends next.
tldr.outcome: Interleaving is required for WebRTC data channels, and an implementation used for them must implement the Weighted Fair Queueing scheduler.

today: RFC 8260 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the I-DATA chunk and the stream schedulers for SCTP.

sections.title: The Head-of-Line Blocking Problem
sections.content:
RFC 4960 SCTP was first imagined for small signaling messages, and fragmentation of larger messages was added late in the design. Sending large messages can cause a form of sender-side head-of-line blocking: a message cannot start because the sender has already begun sending another, possibly large, one.

The RFC blames the Transmission Sequence Number (TSN), which does three jobs: it identifies DATA chunks for reliable transfer, it identifies the order of fragments for reassembly, and it acts as a sequence number allowing up to 216 minus 1 Stream Sequence Numbers outstanding. Because all fragments of a message must have consecutive TSNs, messages cannot be mixed.

This document adds the I-DATA chunk to allow interleaving, and defines several stream schedulers that give streams different relative treatment. The interleaving of user messages is required for WebRTC data channels.
sections.eli5: Imagine a conveyor belt where a huge box has to go first and everything behind it waits. The fix is to let small boxes slip in between pieces of the huge one.

sections.title: The I-DATA Chunk
sections.content:
The I-DATA chunk keeps the properties of the DATA chunk but drops the Stream Sequence Number (SSN) and adds two fields: the Message Identifier (MID) and the Fragment Sequence Number (FSN). Its header is 20 bytes, 4 bytes more than the DATA chunk header, and its chunk type is 64.

The MID is the same for every fragment of a user message and, for ordered messages, also decides delivery order. The sender keeps two independent counters per outgoing stream, one for ordered and one for unordered messages, both starting at 0 and rising by 1 per message. The FSN numbers the fragments of one message from 0, and it shares a 32-bit slot with the Payload Protocol Identifier: if the B bit is set the field holds the PPID, otherwise it holds the FSN.

The flag bits are the same as for DATA: I (do not delay the SACK), U (unordered), B (first fragment) and E (last fragment). The sender MUST NOT have more than 231 minus 1 messages per direction of ordering in flight on a stream, nor more than 231 minus 1 fragments of one message in flight.
sections.eli5: Each piece of a message gets a sticker with the message's name and a piece number, so the receiver can put the pieces together even if they arrive mixed with other messages.

sections.title: Negotiating Interleaving
sections.content:
An endpoint advertises support by listing I-DATA in the Supported Extensions Parameter defined in RFC 5061. Interleaving is in effect only if both endpoints list it. Once negotiated, I-DATA chunks MUST be used for all user messages and DATA chunks MUST NOT be; if it is not negotiated, the reverse holds.

An endpoint using the sockets API of RFC 6458 MUST NOT indicate support unless the application has asked for it, because the application must be able to handle interleaved messages on reception. An implementation also has to let associations that use DATA chunks and associations that use I-DATA chunks coexist.

If a DATA chunk arrives on an association that negotiated I-DATA (or the other way round), the receiver MUST abort the association with an ABORT chunk, which MAY carry the Protocol Violation error cause.
sections.eli5: Both sides have to say yes to the new way of sending, like two friends agreeing to use a secret code. If one of them uses the wrong code, the conversation is cut off.

sections.title: Sender and Receiver Behavior
sections.content:
The sender uses the FSN, not the TSN, to show which fragment it is sending. The first fragment MUST have the B bit, the last MUST have the E bit, and the others MUST have neither. Congestion control and receiver window rules from RFC 4960 still apply. Each I-DATA chunk uses a single TSN, assigned late, so chunks from other streams can sit between the fragments of a big message.

Interleaving works only between different streams. The sender MUST NOT process more than one user message at a time within a stream, though it MAY process several messages on different streams. It MUST assign TSNs so the receiver can make progress; one way is to give later fragments higher TSNs and send them in sequence.

The receiver finds the stream from the Stream Identifier, uses the U bit to tell ordered from unordered, finds the message by MID and reassembles with the FSN. It MUST NOT assume anything about how the sender assigned TSNs. A message with both B and E set is not fragmented.
sections.eli5: Pieces from different people's orders can be mixed on the belt, but one person's own orders still go one at a time.

sections.title: Interaction with Other SCTP Extensions
sections.content:
With the Partial Reliability extension (RFC 3758), the I-FORWARD-TSN chunk (type 194) MUST be used instead of FORWARD-TSN. It replaces the 16-bit SSN with the 32-bit MID and adds a U bit so the largest skipped MID can be given for unordered messages too. FORWARD-TSN MUST go with DATA and I-FORWARD-TSN with I-DATA, and the wrong pairing leads to an ABORT, as for DATA and I-DATA.

With Stream Reconfiguration (RFC 6525), when the SSN is reset the two MID counters MUST be reset to 0. The RFC adds that most schedulers, especially all those supporting interleaving, need late TSN assignment, which an implementation of RFC 6525 has to handle. Future SCTP extensions MUST describe how they interfere with I-DATA.
sections.eli5: Other add-ons to the protocol have to learn the new labels too, so the old and new systems are never mixed on one connection.

sections.title: Stream Schedulers
sections.content:
A stream scheduler decides which outgoing stream sends next. The choice is made at the sender only; nothing signals it to the receiver. An implementation MAY implement any subset, but if it is used for WebRTC data channels it MUST implement the Weighted Fair Queueing scheduler.

  • First-come, first-served: passes messages through in the order the application delivered them.
  • Round-robin: cycles around non-empty stream queues, fair by number of messages without interleaving and by number of I-DATA chunks with it.
  • Round-robin per packet: switches stream only when starting a new packet and bundles chunks of one stream per packet, so a lost packet affects a single stream.
  • Priority-based: strict priorities per stream; with interleaving, big low-priority messages do not delay high-priority ones.
  • Fair capacity: aims for equal capacity per stream by looking at message lengths; details are implementation dependent.
  • Weighted fair queueing: capacity follows per-stream weights, so a stream with n times the weight should get n times the capacity.
sections.eli5: A scheduler is a rule for whose turn it is: take turns, let VIPs go first, or give bigger shares to some people.

sections.title: Socket API Notes
sections.content:
This informational section extends the sockets API of RFC 6458. When interleaving is used, the lower 16 bits of the MID fill the SSN field in the existing receive structures. A new SCTP_ASSOC_SUPPORTS_INTERLEAVING value should appear in the sac_info of an association-change notification when both peers support I-DATA.

Three socket options are added: SCTP_INTERLEAVING_SUPPORTED, SCTP_STREAM_SCHEDULER and SCTP_STREAM_SCHEDULER_VALUE. An application using interleaving should also set the fragment interleave level to 2 with SCTP_FRAGMENT_INTERLEAVE; failure to do so can possibly lead to application deadlock. Because the default level is not 2, interleaving is disabled by default. For the priority scheduler, a higher assigned value means a lower priority and the default 0 is the highest.
sections.eli5: Programs get switches to turn the new feature on and pick the rule for taking turns.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document adds no security considerations beyond those of RFC 4960 and RFC 6458. It does note that the application must consent to the more complex reassembly, and with interleaving it must provide a reassembly buffer for each incoming stream. It has to protect itself against these buffers using too many resources. Without interleaving only one reassembly buffer per association is needed, though excessive resource use still has to be guarded against.
sections.eli5: With more pieces arriving mixed up, you need more trays to sort them, and you must not let strangers fill every tray.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Chunk length in bytes, excluding padding.

fields.name: Message Identifier
fields.desc: Same for all fragments of a message.

fields.name: PPID / FSN
fields.desc: PPID if B is set, otherwise the fragment number.

items.label: Fair capacity
items.desc: Equal capacity per stream (the socket API names it SCTP_SS_FB).

items.label: Weighted fair queueing
items.desc: Capacity by per-stream weight; required for WebRTC data channels.
